extracted.intended_audience: regulated businesses (employers, franchisees, contractors), labor unions, labor/management attorneys, SBA Office of Advocacy, and regulatory commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (FRFA) and accompanying explanations for the NLRB's final rule on the joint-employer standard, including the Board's responses to public comments about costs, conflicts, and affected small entities. Focuses on what must be included in an FRFA and the Board's methodology and legal reasoning for assessing impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: FRFA requirement under the RFA
rubrics_metrics.description: The Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) requires an agency promulgating a final rule to prepare a Final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (FRFA) when the regulation will have a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities; an agency is not required to prepare a FRFA if the Agency head certifies that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities (5 U.S.C. 601-612; 5 U.S.C. 605(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Board believed the rule would not have a significant economic impact, it nevertheless published an FRFA to respond to comments. Agencies must follow RFA procedural requirements when a FRFA is required, including soliciting and considering public comment in the IRFA stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'significant economic impact' and agency discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: The RFA does not define either 'significant economic impact' or 'substantial number of small entities.' In the absence of statutory specificity, what is 'significant' will vary depending on the economics of the industry or sector to be regulated; the agency is in the best position to gauge small-entity impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may apply industry- and sector-specific economic judgment in determining significance; courts defer to agencies on these factual determinations unless arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: FRFA must state the need for and objectives of the rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The FRFA must include a 'Statement of the Need for, and Objectives of, the Rule.' For this rule, the final rule establishes the standard for determining joint-employer status under the NLRA and is intended to ground the joint-employer standard in common-law agency principles and provide guidance about rights and responsibilities when more than one statutory employer possesses or exercises authority to control employees' essential terms and conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An adequate FRFA should explain why the rule is necessary, what it seeks to accomplish, and how the rule's substantive provisions (e.g., defining critical elements and enumerating determining factors) accomplish those objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: FRFA must describe significant public comments, agency assessment, and changes
rubrics_metrics.description: The FRFA must include 'a Statement of the Significant Issues Raised by the Public Comments in Response to the Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis, a Statement of the Assessment of the Agency of Such Issues, and a Statement of any Changes Made in the Proposed Rule as a Result of Such Comments.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency should explicitly respond to comments on costs, compliance burdens, conflicts, and alternatives—and state whether and how the final rule was changed in response. The Board uses this section to address criticisms about estimated reading time and wage-rate inputs, among other issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct compliance costs — scope and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the RFA, 'other compliance requirements' (and thus direct compliance costs) include reporting, recordkeeping, capital costs for equipment to meet regulatory requirements, costs of modifying processes and procedures to comply, lost sales and profits, changes in market competition, extra costs associated with taxes or fees, and hiring employees dedicated to compliance (SBA Guide examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this rule the Board identified the only identifiable direct compliance cost as reading and understanding the substantive changes to the joint-employer standard. Agencies should categorize costs as direct (compliance-based) versus indirect/speculative and support any direct-cost estimates with appropriate data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of empirical national data (BLS) for wage-rate cost estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board relied on the Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) national average wage rates (e.g., for labor relations specialists and private industry employees) to estimate the cost of time spent reading or consulting about the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may rely on BLS national averages to estimate wage-hour costs for compliance unless commenters provide evidence showing a superior, representative alternative. Surveys or matrices focused on atypically expensive markets (Laffey Matrix, Bloomberg rates) or non-representative convenience samples (Clio) are insufficient without methodology demonstrating national representativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating reading and attorney-consultation time
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board estimated one hour to read the final rule and one hour for an attorney consult (with further adjustment to add an additional hour for a human-resources/labor-relations specialist to meet with the attorney). The Board will not change such time estimates absent empirical evidence to the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may rely on prior IRFA familiarization-time estimates and on reasonable average assumptions across millions of entities; commenters disputing such time estimates must provide empirical support. The agency may adjust estimates where comments demonstrate a factual basis for change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude indirect, speculative, and avoidance costs from direct-cost calculus
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs associated with discretionary actions (avoidance costs), speculative downstream effects (e.g., lost entrepreneurial opportunities, decreased support from franchisors), or increased litigation/insurance are indirect or speculative and are not 'direct compliance costs' required to be counted under the RFA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The RFA, caselaw (Mid-Tex Electric Cooperative; White Eagle; Colorado State Banking Board; Cement Kiln Recycling Coalition), and SBA guidance confine agency analysis to likely direct burdens of compliance, not all conceivable indirect effects. Agencies need not convert rulemaking into 'a massive exercise in economic modeling' of every indirect effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for identifying conflicts with other federal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: For section 603(b)(5) purposes, rules are 'conflicting' when they impose two conflicting regulatory requirements on the same classes of industry (SBA Guide at 40).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters claiming conflicts must identify the conflicting authorities and explain the inconsistency; agencies should explain why differences in statutory text, purpose, and legislative history can produce different meanings across laws and why the final rule does or does not create an unworkable conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint-employer essential terms categories (§103.40(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule provides an exhaustive list of the seven categories of terms and conditions of employment that will be considered essential for the joint-employer inquiry (§103.40(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FRFA should point to where the rule enumerates critical elements (the seven categories) so regulated parties can determine in advance whether actions are likely to result in a joint-employer finding; providing clear categorical guidance reduces uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control standard includes exercised, unexercised, or indirect authority (§103.40(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish joint-employer status, the common-law employer must possess exercised or unexercised authority to control, or exercise the power to control indirectly (such as through an intermediary), an essential term or condition of employment (§103.40(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule clarifies that mere ability (even if unexercised) to control essential terms may be relevant; agencies should explain how indirect or reserved authority is assessed under common-law agency principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrelevance of immaterial matters (§103.40(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of an entity's control over matters that are immaterial to the existence of an employment relationship under common-law agency principles and that do not bear on employees' essential terms and conditions of employment is not relevant to the determination of joint-employer status (§103.40(f)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FRFA and rule text should clarify that peripheral or purely administrative controls are not indicative of joint-employer status, helping regulated parties distinguish relevant from irrelevant evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology for estimating number of affected small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate universe using Census Bureau business counts (e.g., number of firms with employees), then use Agency case filings (representation petitions and unfair labor practice charges alleging joint-employer relationships) to estimate frequency and the subset of entities most directly impacted; where data are lacking, make and disclose reasonable assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board used multi-year case data to calculate percentages of firms affected (.028% over five years; .015% over a later four-year period) and explained assumptions where exact jurisdictional exclusions or size breakdowns were unavailable. Agencies should disclose methods and assumptions when extrapolating from incomplete data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of small-entity categories most likely impacted
rubrics_metrics.description: The FRFA should identify categories of small businesses likely to be impacted; the Board identified five: (1) contractors/subcontractors; (2) temporary help service suppliers; (3) temporary help service users; (4) franchisees; and (5) labor unions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sector-specific discussion explaining why those categories face greater joint-employer exposure (e.g., shared workspaces, supply of workers, franchisor operational control), and, where possible, quantify counts or proportions using available data (NAICS, Census, SBA thresholds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of significant alternatives to minimize economic impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the RFA the agency should consider significant alternatives that would accomplish the objectives of the statute while minimizing economic impacts on small entities; the SBA Office of Advocacy expressly encouraged such consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should analyze and explain alternatives considered (and reasons for rejecting or adopting them) in the FRFA or related sections (the Board references Section VI.6 for such analysis), even if commenters do not provide concrete alternative proposals.
